PyTorch Conv1d uses cross-correlation: kernel taps are not reversed. For stride=1, groups=1, dilation d and K taps, set P=d*(K-1), then xp=F.pad(x_BCL,(P,0)). Its BLC output equals sum(F.linear(xp[:,:,k*d:k*d+L].transpose(1,2), weight[:,:,k], None) for k in range(K)) + bias. Tap 0 sees the oldest position; tap K-1 sees the current position. Add bias once after summation. Preserve the original Parameter objects and use differentiable slices/transposes without detach or tensor reconstruction; autograd then accumulates input and weight gradients. Mathematical equivalence does not imply bitwise equality across GPU kernels. These formulas follow the documented [Conv1d](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Conv1d.html), [padding](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.nn.functional.pad.html), [linear](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.nn.functional.linear.html), and [autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/notes/autograd.html) semantics.

A vectorized construction is S=xp.unfold(2,P+1,1)[...,::d].permute(0,2,3,1), giving B,L,K,Cin. For input-dependent scalar gates G shaped B,L,K, compute torch.einsum('blkc,ock->blo', S*G.unsqueeze(-1), weight)+bias. Alternatively flatten gated S over K,Cin and use one F.linear with weight.permute(0,2,1).reshape(Cout,-1). Both are derived from documented [unfold](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.Tensor.unfold.html) and [einsum](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.einsum.html) operations. Gates must use only causal features; all-one gates recover the original convolution. Practical inference: vectorization avoids K Python-dispatched projections but may materialize B*L*K*Cin intermediates; a small-K loop can remain competitive. Budget feasibility requires timing representative forward/backward batches and checking output/gradient agreement before full training.
